p: The plight of the visible church is a perilous one. The good ship Zion sails a stormy sea and there is no calm in sight. All about us, at home and abroad, the rumblings are portentous. Almost everywhere the heavy hand of oppression fetters the faithful. In many places across the world the visible church is all but destroyed, and the handwriting is on the wall in this Land of the free and home of the brave.

When will we learn that the events of one generation are but the history of a previous generation repeating itself? And that what has happened before can, does and will happen again? Wherever and whenever the church has failed to save the people, the people have destroyed the church. That is to say that the visible church is destroyed and the faithful maintain their devotion amid fierce and frightful persecution. Testimony is sealed in death and once again the blood of the martyrs becomes the seed of the church.

The supreme task of the church is that of saving men. The power to accomplish this is to be found in the separation of the church from the world. Long ago the Lord of the Church said to His disciples, "Ye are not of the world,... even as lani not of the world." In the world?-Yes. But not of it! The supremacy of the church is the separation of the church. This otherworldness is the fulcrum upon which rests the lever to move men Godward.

The church is the only institution that makes any attempt to save men. It is the only human agency God has for the reclamation of the erring. If the church bogs down here all will be lost. The evangel of redeeming love is to be proclaimed through the agency of a God-filled church which is passing the days of her sojourn in conscious communion with her living Lord.

When the church walks hand in hand with the world; when its members live, act and talk as does the worldling; when the observer can see no difference between the professor of grace and the nonprofessor; when those professing godliness run with the world to sinful places of amusement which are but schemes of the devil to damn the unwary; when those who call themselves Christians frequent dens of iniquity; when the church resorts to unscriptural methods to raise money for the cause of God because church members are too selfish to support that which they profess to love; when the prayer meeting is abandoned and the Sunday night service is forsaken-when the foregoing is true (and who can say we have overstated it?), what result can there be but that an unbelieving and cynical world will rise up and cast out the church, not because of what we professed but because we only professed it, Let us not be fooled It can happen here

What is the cure? Is there one? Yes! If the church will seek the presence and power of God; if it will regain and retain its pristine purity; if it will allow the Spirit of God to be resident in and president of its redemptive activities; if the prayer meetings will again be filled with the faithful; if pulpit and pew will labor together for a mighty revival of genuine, all-wool-anda-yard-wide religion; if everybody everywhere that names the name of the Lord will depart from iniquity; if God is honored and the gospel proclaimed-the church will be saved, thousands will be swept into the Kingdom and there will come to our fair land a better day.
It is revival or revolution, Christ or chaos, religion or ruin. We stand at the crossroads. Which shall it be?

One has observed that the word conscience is used some thirty times in the New Testament and that there are probably as many definitions of the word. (And equally as many smart sayings concerning its use and abuse.) Every physical sense has been enlisted to illustrate this faculty of God in the soul,

Permit a definition: Conscience is that medium through which is transmitted the moral judgments and imperatives of God. A breakdown reveals the word science,“to which is attached the prefix con.”Science“is knowledge;”con is the "with“of association and relationship.”Conscience, then, is the moral knowledge of myself with, or in relation to, another. That Other is God. The "con“implies a second presence, God.”Conscience“means”Thou God seest me."

Now see how it looks: The accuracy of the „ science „ depends upon the atmosphere of the relationship. If the eye is evil (the medium diseased), the whole body is filled with darkness (the image is distorted)..

Everywhere we see the lowering of standards upon tile part of professed Christians. Such is excused on the plea that conscience does not protest. Often this is true. Because the vertical communion is spotty and broken, the horizontal concepts are superficial and feeble. The impoverishment of one is the impairment of the other. Thus because a marred lens has stirred the impression knowledge is but a caricature.

Upon the highest scriptural level fear is not the word for a slavish dread. Rather is it a holy sensitivity with finger-tip perceptions of the Divine. Let us take our bearings. Light is light from conversion to coronation. The building of things once destroyed marks one a transgressor, and what poses as the revelation of new light may be but the return of other-day darkness. It may be wise to examine the court before we consider the case. There is a disease of the eye in which the fluid dries and the eye is left blind. It is the constant cleansing of the eye by the fluid that makes possible the sharp focus of the picture. It is only as the medium of fellowship with God is undisturbed that the image of moral perception can remain undistorted.

Cowardice asks, Is it safe? Expediency, Is it good politics? Vanity, Is it popular? Conscience, Is it right? For the earnest believer it is ever thus. There are no neutral shades and no middle ground between right and wrong.

As the apostle bared the fabric of his life to the scrutiny of his conscience, he found no "fleshly wisdom“or clever pretense or cheap deceit. Rather was there the simplicity of singlehearted allegiance to the divine standard. Simplicity is not synonynnous with silliness. It is the word for a single layer or fold of cloth and is the opposite of duplicity (many layers or folds). Placed alongside the sun-drenched”sincerity of God" his life matched the light from the throne.
Only by the constant and vigorous exercise of living up to all our light can we have a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men."-H. J. s.

What is the standard by which true riches are measured? For the most part the standard is things: what the eye can see and the hand hold. And the more one can amass of these "things“the richer he is thought to be. If one lacks”things" he is considered poor. So runs the thought of the masses.

But the standard that makes "things" the test of riches is in error. Things can be taken by another-and usually are. The strong are able to hold them for a while, but sooner or later a stronger appears and the transfer is made. The weak and the old must let go.

Again: the market value of things rises or falls according to conditions over which the possessor has no control. Depreciation, the seasons, the law of supply and demand-all these factors are beyond the control of the one who is rich in mere things. Then, too, one must eventually leave "things“and take the long journey to the land where things do not count and where things are not used. One man asked another concerning a third who had recently died,”How much did he leave?" "He left it all," was the illuminating reply. Yes, we cannot hold things for long. Someone else gets them or their value declines or we must leave them.

Wherein do true riches lie? What can we take with us when we are changing worlds? Well, not what one lias but what one is. True riches can never be taken by another. How can the thiering and mercenary steal faith? And hope? And moral rightness? How can another purloin the virtues with which God graces the soul? Who can take from us what we are? By the infinite grace of a good God true riches are as much a part of their possessor as is his eye or foot. To revel in the beauties of a sunset, to appreciate the music of a symphony, to stand atop a mountain and survey the sun-drenched landscape-who can take this from us?

But more: the market value of true riches never declines. When were a sense of humor and a cheerful countenance ever below par? When was there ever a depreciation in the value of faith? When has there been a day when hope was outmoded? Is moral rectitude ever out of season? When did a stock of patience ever fail to pay its owner a dividend? Is the market ever glutted with an overstock of love? Of devotion? Or reverence?

The riches that are true are also abiding. We may take them with us when we leave the world: Faith. Hope. Love. These are the coins of the better land. They make up the currency of the celestial. When one crosses the narrow stream that divides time from eternity he takes with him what he is. We have what we are.

Learn the parable of the unjust steward: He possessed but did not own. He was soon to be dispossessed. Beyond the dispossession there would be sustenance needed for self and dependents. By investing a wealth not his in human personalities he turned present assets into future security. The lesson: By the alchemy of divine grace we may convert material values and human assets into spiritual wealth that will provide for eternal requisites. Yes, by the grace of God, true riches are possible to every son of Adam.-H. J. s.

In the Balance-The Christian World The situation of our world today is so grave that every Anielic:111 must be reficl), to flee facts and be willing to seriously ask himself-"What can I do about it?"
We think the situation boils down to asking yourself this simple question:

Just how important is it to me to be living in what is generally called "a Christian World"? Reply to this question honestly and you will have the answer to where this nation and the world as we know it are headed.

All signs point to another great tragedy in history. Read the history of the rise and fall of the Greek, Roman and French empires and you will recognize so clearly that those same signs are present in our nation today. The tragedy is that in the short space of time since our forefathers founded our nation we see these signs of decay that wrought about the collapse of those modern world empires.

With the firm belief that hard work and real faith in God would bring forth their reward, the Pilgrims laid the foundation from which has grown the richest and most powerful nation in the world today.
This priceless heritage of ours is in danger!

The great advances made in science and technology have wrought to us richness and an master way of living. But man's need today seems to be primarily for the material things of life... such things asa television set, a refrigerator, an automobile. Dozens of other laborsaving devices for our homes are terribly important.
A Bible and a seat in a church seem to have lost their importance. God definitely has been forsake!

What then is happening? No one can deny that there is a serious decline in moral concepts. Too many of us are willing to say that we are Christians, but when it comes to living a Christian life we do so on our own terms.

Sometimes the truth hurts and it makes us ready to deny it, or go into a shell, or try to justify ourselves. Sometimes, thank God, though the truth hurts it brings an awakening and a willingness to do something to set things right. That time is now...it must be now if you, like other men and women, want to safeguard your heritage so that your children will have a better chance to live in peace, happiness and security in a truly Christian world.

We urge our religious leaders to teach if possible with greater wisdom and understanding that moral concepts and faith in God are things worth living and fighting for. We also urge that leaders of religious faiths make greater efforts to bring about a unity of purpose in extending Christian fellowship to all corners of the world.
We urge each American-you and your friends and neighbors-to give a little more of ourselves to God's purpose when He gave you your life.
Is all this possible? It should be simple.

Man has inherited from God the power to do great things. If this inheritance and this latent power that is in every man are harnessed, if the minds and hearts of all men will be moved, the world we want for our children and grandchildren is possible of attainment.
We need not fear a tragedy that can be avoided.
Remembering the past let us all, with courage and high faith in the promise of God, accept this challenge and start today to repair the damage toman's soul.

p: It is one thing to get into the will of God. It is another thing to stand there. It is a place of such restfulness, fruitfulness and victory that Satan will do his utmost to dislodge us. There are not a few who, alas, yield to his seductions, and who never get back again into the garden. If he cannot tempt us out, he will try to drive us out. Skills in the field of science and mechanics have made phenomenal progress in the last fifty years. It is regrettable, however, that the same cannot be said of the areas affecting human relations. Men have put together great engines with tremendous horsepower and speed I that annihilates distance, yet no way has been found to put together the human family so that it can establish a safe and sane social order that functions without discord and war.

In the book of Ecclesiastes (9:18) the writer declared: "Wisdom is better than weapons of war: but one sinner earth-bound man. "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. The man under the sun who had drunk from the cup of pleasure, who lived in the lap of luxury and who knew the security that came from material wealth, said, "All is vanity.“But he wisely declared to men of earth,”Wisdom is better than weapons of war."
Great skills are being invested in the building of in. 0

struments of destruction. We all tremble at the thought of what an atomic or biological war might mean to civilization. Men have tried the League of Nations and now the United Nations, both of which have made some contribution in the field of human relations, but no practical solution has been found. There must be a way without weapons. We need skills, mental energy and spiritual understanding more than ever in our history.

The writer in Ecclesiastes says that one sinner destroyeth much good. One evildoer can destroy the peace and fellowship of the world. In modern times we saw the destructive holocaust that came through the evildoings of Hitler and Mussolini, and the military clique that led Japan into militarism. Now we are suffering from the evil work of another man who continues to slander America and carry on his vicious propaganda, giving the world the impression that our dominating passion is for money and power.

In a much narrower circle we see the effects of the evildoer, ora tale-bearer, that foments discord and oftentimes disrupts whole congregations. Homes are wrecked by the purveyors of gossip. Someone has warned us against being a thoroughfare through which all evil may circulate freely. We must never consent to be the common sewer of the society in which we live and move. When we take away a person's character, we take away his life; for character is the man. When we whisper that a man is not what he ought to be, it is to put a knife to the man's throat.

"Wisdom is better than weapons. What we need is the Wisdom of God, not something but Someone. The wisdom of God is Christ Himself. Man has tried, by his skills applied in many fields, to make the world a safe place in which to live; but all the while he bypasses Christ. We will never come to the age when swords will be beaten into plowshares until we have the Wisdom of God, Christ Himself.

The Church, too, has tried to meet its problems and serve its generation by resorting to the wisdom of man instead of living under the power and leadership of its head, the Lord Jesus Christ. The Church, someone has said, has been more problem-conscious than power-conscious. We should have spent more time with God and man's spiritual nature and less time trying to solve world problems. Christ has shown us that we must begin in the human heart-the need is internal rather than external.

If the church through the centuries had been faithful to its task of world evangelism we would have prepared the hearts of men for the law of love and the reign of peace. It is possible that if we had sent more men and women with their feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace there would have been fewer men going into battle with their feet shod with military boots. What wisdom we might have exhibited had we had a great army through the centuries marching with Christ instead of keeping step to the music of the gods of war. Wisdom is still better than weapons. Divine skills are now needed in every phase of our lives. The world is looking for wise men, but what we need is the Man of Wisdom, the Lord Jesus Christ.-R. R. B.

A very important person in the operation of our railroads is the individual who announces the arrival and the high-ceilinged stations. It has dignity and resonance. Some of the places are inviting-Jacksonville, Palm Beach, Miami, Tucson, Phoenix or points south and west.

We are certain that this work is essential; passengers can easily become confused and take the wrong train, The question that comes to our minds is whether these dispatchers know anything about the places they announce. Have they been there? What is it like "down South"? We've never had the courage to ask these questions for fear we would get the answer, "I don't know, Bud; I've never been there. The confines of their community may be the limit of their travels.

There are stations along the Way of Life that need to be called: Justified by Faith, Saved through the Blood, Filled with the Spirit, Afore than Conquerors, Peace that Passes Understanding. These are areas in the realm of the divine that should be explored. These truths are to be made clear-in the sound of the words and the soundness of the doctrine. But our responsibility does not end there. People may not ask audibly but they are thinking, "What is it like?... Have you been there?“What a tragedy if we must confess,”I don't know. chapters.t: We Must Give Time to God
p: Probably the most widespread and persistent problem to be found among Christians is the problem of retarded spiritual progress. Why, after years of Christian profession, do so many persons fine themselves no further along than when they first belie,ed?

Some would try to dissolve the difficulty by asserting flatly that such persons were never saved; that they had never been truly regenerated. They are simply deceived professors who have stopped short of true conversion.

With a few this may be the answer, and we would accept this explanation as final did we not know that it is never the deceived professor that laments his lack of spiritual growth, but the true Christian who has had a real experience of conversion and who is sure that he is this very moment trusting in Christ for salvation. Uncotinted numbers of such believers are among the disappointed ones who deplore their lack of spiritual growth.

The causes of retarded growth are many. It would not be accurate to ascribe the trouble to one single fault. One there is. however. which is so universal that it may easily be the main cause: failure to gite time to the cultitation of the knowledge of God.

The temptation to make our relation to God judicial instead of personal is very strong. Believing for salvation has these days been reduced to a once-done act that requires no further attention. The young believer becomes aware of an act performed rather than of a living Saviour to be followed and adored.

The Christian is strong or weak depending upon lion, closely he has cultivated the knowledge of God. Paul was anything but an advocate of the once-done, automatic school of Christianity. He devoted his whole Life to the art of knowing Christ. "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ.... That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death... I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus " (Phil. 8: 8, 10, 14).

Progress in the Christian life is exactly equal to the growing knowledge we gain of the Triune God in personal experience. And such experience requires a whole life devoted to it and plenty of time spent at the holy task of cultivating God. God can be known satisfactorily only as we devote time to Him. Without meaning to do it we have written our serious fault into our book titles and gospel songs. "A little talk with Jesus,“we sing, and we call our books”God's Minute,“or something else as revealing. The Christian who is satisfied to give God His”minute“and to have”a little talk with Jesus" is the same one who shows lip at the evangelistic service weeping over his retarded spiritual growth and begging the evangelist to show him the way out of his difficulty.

We may as well accept it, there is no short cut to sanctity. Even the erises that come in the spiritual life are usually the result of long periods of thought and prayerful meditation. As the wonder grows more and more dazzling there is likely to occur a crisis of revolutionizing proportions, This may be carelessly set down to a sudden moment of spiritual experience unless we remember that that crisis was an outgrowth, a sudden sweet explosion, an uprushing of the water that had been increasing its pressure within until we could no longer contain it, Back of it all was the slow buildup and preparation that comes from waiting upon God.
A thousand distractions would woo us awar from

thoughts of God, but if we are wise we will sternly put them from us and make room for the King and time to entertain Him. Anything else may be neglected with but little loss to the spiritual life, but to neglect communion with God is to hurt ourselves where we cannot afford it. God will submit Himself to our efforts to know Him. The Bible tells us how; it is altogether a matter of whether or not we are determined.

Basically, the problem is a spiritual one. Jean Nicholas Grou, who lived in the eighteenth century (1781-1808): wrote a searching chapter on the subject, and we present it on page 5 of this issue. The question -and the answer-remains the same today.

chapters.t: We Must not Defend, but Attack!
p: Too many of our religious convictions are negative. We act not from a positive conviction that something is right, but from a feeling that the opposite is wrong.
We become allergic to certain beliefs and practices and react violently from them. Thus our reactions become actions; we are driven to our positions by the enemy rather than led to them by the truth.

The bad reasoning back of this kind of thing is the assumption that if a man is wrong on one thing he is wrong on everything, so that if a liberal ora cultist is known to favor a belief we shy away from the belief not because we know why it is wrong but because we know who holds it. We are thus always on the defensive; we back into our positions like stubborn horses rather than walk into them face forward like obedient sheep. The way to be right, so we reason, is to watch the enemy, discover what he favors, and then choose the opposite.

That many of our hotly defended beliefs are no more than reactions from what we consider false doctrine it would not be difficult to prove. The doctrine of justification by works (itself a serious error), for instance, has driven some teachers to espouse the equally damaging error of salvation without works. To many persons the very thought of "works" is repugnant because of its association with the effete Judaism of New Testament times and the Romanism of more recent days. The upshot of the matter is that we have salvation without righteousness and right doctrine without right deeds. Grace is twisted out of its moral context and made the cause of lowered standards of conduct in the Church.

Again, the fear of "legalism“has driven some of God, S good people to positions so grotesque as to be ridiculous. Some years ago in a church paper we came across an example of this negative kind of doctrine. In order to make clear the difference between law and grace, a writer argued that if a murderer came to him and inquired how to be saved he would not dare say,”Turn away from your old life, cease to commit murder and believe on Jesus Christ.“That, said the writer, would be mixing law and grace. All he could say to be scriptural, he reasoned, would be”Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved." Such unholy teaching could not possibly come direct from the Scriptures; it could only result from the writer's frightened retreat from the error of salvation by works.

We have noticed very much the same thing in our standard attitude toward science, evolution and various current philosophies which we believe to be contrary to or unsympathetic with the Christian faith. Our reaction to these enemies is one of blind flight. We use up a lot of ammunition, but we waste it in a rear guard action that can at best only slow up what is too patently a retreat.

Now, it is our firm faith that Christianity can stand on its own legs. Christ does not need our nervous defense. The Church must not allow herself to be maneuvered into fighting her enemy's war, letting the unbelieving world decide what she is to believe and where and when she is to act. Just as long as she does this she is falling short of her privileges in Christ Jesus.
Ye shall receive power, said our Lord to His dis-

ciples, and "power“means”ability to do." It is God's purpose to give us ample power to carry the fight to the enemy instead of sitting passively by and allowing the enemy to carry the fight to us. If anyone is to go on the defensive it should never be the Church, The truth is self-validating and self-renewing; its whole psychology is that of attack. Its own vigorous attack is all the defense it needs.

Could it be that the deep cause behind all this frightened defensive action on the part of the evangelicals today is the failure of so many leaders to have a true spiritual experience of their own? It is hard to see how any man who has seen heaven opened and has ever be uncertain about the message he is to proclaim.
DR. JOHN W. BRADBURY, editor, Watcliman-Examiner:

How does God forgive sin? Were we to give the numerous explanations we have listened to in churches, the result would be quite confusing. Some indicate that God will forgive sin unconditionally. It all seems plausible and easy. "

We sing, "Jesus paid it all, and then tell people that all they have to do is come and get salvation and heaven. In some senses this may be true, but it ought to be more fully explained, for God never forgives anti tuan until he believes. What is the sinner to believe?... The Bible gives the clearest answer, that believing in Christ carries with it the repentance of the believer in respect to the righteousness and holiness of God. The sinner believes God to be right and himself wrong. He assents to the supreme will of God, or lie does not believe at all. Unless he takes God's side against his sin, can he be said to 'be a believer? On what grounds? God has revealed Himself as the supreme Ruler, as holy, and we are expected to believe Him to be such and act accordingly. There can be no forgiveness until we turn our backs on sinful ways.

chapters.t: The Second-Best Book for a Christian
p: In order to express myself more freely on a matter that lies very near to my heart I shall waive the rather stilted editorial we and speak in the first person.

The matter I have in mind is the place of the hymnbook in the devotional life of the Christian. For purposes of inward devotion there is Only One book to be placed before the hymnal, and that of course is the Bible. I say without qualification, after the Sacred Scriptures the next best companion for the soul is a good hymnal.

For the child of God the Bible is the book of all books. to be reverenced, loved, pored over endlessly and feasted upon as living bread and manna for the soul. It is the first-best book, the olill/ indispensable book. To ignore it or neglect it is to doom our minds to error and our hearts to starvation.
After the Bible, the hymbook is next. And remember. I do not say a songbook nor a book of gospel songs, but a real hymnal containing the cream of the great Christian hymns left to us by the ages.

One of the serious weaknesses of present-day evangelicalism is the mechanical quality of its thinking. A utilitarian Christ has taken the place of the radiant Saviour of other and happen times. This Christ is able to save, it is true, but He is thought to do so in a practical across-the-counter manner, paying our debt and tearing off the receipt like a court clerk acknowledging a paid-up fine. A bank teller psychology characterizes much of the religious thinking in our little gospel circle. The tragedy of it is that it is truth without being all the truth.

If modern Christians are to approach the spiritual greatness of Bible saints, or know the inward delights of the saints of post-Biblical times, they must correct this imperfect view and cultivate the beauties of the Lord our God in sweet, personal experience. In achieving such. happy state a good hymnbook will help more than any other book in the world except the Bible itself.

A great hymn embodies the priest concentrated thoughts of some lofty saint who may have long ago gone from the earth and left little or nothing behind him except that hymn. Toreador sing a true hymn is to join in the act of worship with a great and gifted soul in his moments of intimate devotion. It is to hear a lover of Christ explaining to his Saviour why he loves Him; it is to listen in without embarrassment on the softest whisperings of undying love between the bride and the heavenly Bridegroom.

Sometimes our hearts are strangely stubborn and will not soften nor grow tender no matter how much praying we do. At such times it is often found that the reading or singing of a good hymn will melt the ice jam and start the inward affections to flowing. That is one of the uses of the hymnbook. Human emotions are curious and difficult to arouse, and there is always a danger that they may be aroused by the wrong means and for the wrong reasons.

The human heart is like an orchestra, and it is important that when the soul starts to sound its melodies a David ora Bernard ora Watts ora Wesley should be on the podium. Constant devotion to the hymnbook will guarantee this happy event and will, conversely, protect the heart from being led by evil conductors.

Every Christian should have lying beside his Bible a copy of some standard hymnbook. He should read out of one and sing out of the other, and he will be surprised and delighted to discover how much they are alike. Gifted Christian poets have in many of our great hymns set truth to music. Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley (possibly above all others) were able to marry the harp of David to the Epistles of Paul and give us singing doctrine, ecstatic theology that delights while it enlightens.

For those who want to pursue this subject further I would recommend any of the following books: The Hymnary of the United Church of Canada, the Presbyterian Book of Praise, ora copy of the old Methodist Hymn Book. Since I am not a musician, I prefer the books without the musical score. Having a fair memory, I can usually recall a tune (whether it is correct or not matters very little for I speak now of the hymnbook to be used in private devotions), and it is surprising how many lofty hymns will fit into the few tunes with which I am familiar. If the meter of some great spiritual gem does not suggest a tune I already know then it is always a simple matter to improvise one; nobody but God is hearing, anyway, and He is not concerned so much with the tune as with the heart.
There is an exquisite fitness in our celebrating the resurrection of Christ in the spring.

When nature is waking to life again after her lona winter of sleep, it is then that the thoughts of Christians everywhere are turned to the wonder of the Saviour's coming out of the tomb after His ordeal with sin and death. Christ's resurrection was an act once accomplished at a given moment in history. It does not in any sense depend upon seasons or celebrations, nor does the miracle of the springtime add anything to the glory of the once-done deed. The workings of God in nature do, however. cast a warm light upon His workings in redemption and the springtime of life in the earth illustrates the miracle of life in the new creation.

Nicholas Herman at eighteen years of age was wrought to Christ by seeing in midwinter a dry and leaftess tree and thinking what a change the spring would make in its condition. He reasoned that if God could make such a difference in a tree He could change the heart of a sinner, too, and God did not fail him. His heart was changed and his life was from that day devoted to the service of Christ. Uncounted thousands of Christians over the last three hundred years have thanked God that young Nicholas saw that leafless tree.

It takes some faith to stand in a winter landscape surrounded by the chill silence of snow and ice and believe that in a few short weeks every trace of frost will be gone, that the snow-covered hills will be dressed in green and the ice-locked streams will be running swift and free again in the summer sun. Yet our confidence is never disappointed. "The earth is the Lord's“and always He”reneweth the face of the earth."

It is hard to imagine anything less hopeful than the sight of a burial. When the body of Christ was taken down from the cross, wrapped in a clean linen cloth and laid in a new tomb hewn out in the rock, how many who looked on had the faith to hope that inside three days this dead Mail should be walking again among men, alive forevermore? But so it came to pass. Aaron's rod burned. The leafless tree on which the Saviour died sprang into bloom. What had been stark death before became life at the touch of God. and the rude gibbet became the gate to everlasting life.

The resurrection of Christ, we repeat, is a once - done act. "Christ being raised from the dead diet no more; death hath no more dominion over him." But Christians die. Every day the bones of believing men and women are taken out to the cemetery and laid to rest with many a quiet song and soft repetitions of Scripture texts. No matter how we may try to avoid the facts, Christians die as their Lord died before them. Their cold helplessness, their sudden strange silence which no pleadings of anguished love can break, their apparent defeat by the relentless forces of nature-all this stuns the heart and (if the truth were told) arouses many an unconfessed fear that this is all, that we have seen our friends for the last time. It is winter when we lay our loved ones down. So it seems to the natural heart. So it must have appeared to some of the Thessalonian Christians. Why otherwise should it have been necessary that Paul write them and exhort them to sorrow not as others which had no hope?

One thing the resurrection teaches us is that we must not trust to appearances. The leaftess tree says by its appearance that there will be no second spring; the body in Joseph's new tomb appears to signify the end of everything for Christ and His disciples; the limp form of a newlv-dead believer suggests everlasting defeat. Yet how wrong are all these appearances. The tree will bloom again. Christ arose the third day according to the Scriptures; and the Christian will rise again
Faith can afford to accept the appearance of defeat, knowing the true believer cannot be defeated finally. „ „
Because I live, ye shall live also. That is the message of Easter. What a blessed message for the whole world if men would only believe it.
John of the Cross shows why we should forsake all things for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ:

"All the beauty of the creation, in comparison with the infinite beauty of God, is stipreme deformity.... All the grace and comeliness of creation, compared with the grace of God, is supreme disgrace and supreme disfavor.... All the goodness of the whole

world together, in comparison with the infinite goodness of God. is wickedness rather than goodness.... All the wisdom of the world, and all human cunning, compared with the infinite wisdom of God, is simple and supreme ignorance.... 11 the riches and © alorv of the whole creation compared with the true ric·lies, ~which is God. is supreme poverty and meanness, and he who sets his heart upon them, is, in God's sight, supremely poor and mean, and can never attain to the blessed estate of riches and glory, which is the transformation of the soul in God."

This world is a form; our bones are forms; and no visible acts of devotion can be without forms. But!/ct the less form in religion the better, since God is a spirit. For the more mental our worship the more adequate to the nature of God; the more silent, the more suitable to the language of a Spirit.- Willing PENN.

chapters.t: During the early days of the wilderness…
p: During the early days of the wilderness journey of the Israelites an odd and significant transaction took place between Moses and an in-law named Hobab.

"And Moses said unto Hobab...We are journeying unto the place of which the Lord said, I will give it you: come thou with us, and we will do thee good." Hobab remonstrated that he did not want to go, but
Moses insisted: Leave us not, I pray thee; forasmuch as thou knowest how we are to encamp in the wilderness, and thou majesty be to us instead of eyes" C Num. 10:29-82).

Imagine! Moses hired a guide to lead Israel through the wilderness! The circumstances being what they were, this seems almost incredible, but after all Moses was a man capable of making mistakes like the rest of us. And hiding Tiobab was a serious mistake. Here is why:

God had already told Moses that He himself would lead Israel into the promised land. "Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared“(Ex. 28:20). God had also provided the wondrous cloud and fire to lead them (Num, 9.15-28). Furthermore, in the very chapter that tells of Moses' effort to enlist Hobab's aid it is written,”And they departed from the mount of the Lord three days' journey: and the ark of the covenant of the Lord went before them in the three days journey, to search out a resting place for them" (Num. 10:33). So through the divinely appointed angel and by means of the Ark and the cloudy pillar God Himself was guiding Israel through the wilderness, What need then had they of Hobab's eyes?

Hobab was not to blame for his part in this strange doing, but his presence adder nothing to the safety of the marching army; and there is reason to believe that he may have been a spiritual stumbling block both to Moses and to the nation of Israel. The more they trusted to Hobab the less they trusted in God. And that was bad for Israel.

The Church also has her appointed Guide to lead her in her earthly journey. "But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you (John 14:26). "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sous of God" (Rom. 8: 14). These and a wealth of other Scriptures assure us that we are under the direct care of the Holy Spirit. Safety and fruitfulness require only that we accept the leadership of God. Blessing lies in the way of submission and obedience.

What need do we have of Hobab's eyes? Surely none at all. Yet the Church has a whole army of Hobabs to which it looks eagerly for guidance and leadership. That Hobab has no place in the divine plan never seems to matter at all. That Hobab is an intruder, that his eyes are not sharp enough to search out the path, that he is altogether superfluous and actually in the way is passed over by almost everyone. God seems so far away, the Bible is such an old book, faith makes such heavy demands upon our flesh, and Hobab is so near at hand and so real and easy to lean on-so we act like men of earth instead of like men of heaven, and Hobab gets the job.

Now, who is Hobab? and how can we identify him? The answer is easy. Hobab is anything gratuitously introduced into the holy work of God which does not have Biblical authority for its existence. At first this new thing may seem innocent enough and even look like an improvement over the Biblical pattern; and because it is new it is sure to catch on fast and spread quickly among the churches. We Christians are soon playing "follow the leader," trotting along docilely behind Hobab and justifying his presence by appealing to his popularity. Anyone as popular as Hobab cannot be wrong, no matter how far he may be from the Tford of God,

Hobab is not an individual. He is whatever takes our attention from the cloud and fire; he is whatever causes us to lean less heavily upon God and look less trustfully to the guiding Spirit. Each one of us must look out for him in our own life and in our church. And when we discover him we must get rid of him right away.

" For tbits saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, those nalne is Holy; I dwell in the high and hol!/ place, icith him also that is of a contrite and hinnble spirit, to retire the spirit of the humble, and to price the heart Of the contrite ones (Isa. 57:15).

In this verse is described the most sweeping circumference in all the universe. God is above the circle of the earth inhabiting eternity. far above all might and dominion and principalities and powers. Everything is beneath Him, and yet God thus exalted has promised to dwell with them of a humble and contrite spirit.

The words contrition, humility, tenderness, brokenness, are bedfellows, describing that frame of heart enjoined in the Beatitudes and approved by the Blessed One Himself. Thomas h Kempis said, "I had rather feel contrition than know the definition thereof. So the broken spirit that God blesses and dwells with is something we know and feel by spiritual intuition rather than by technical definition. It may suffice to say that brokenness which goes hand in hand with contrition and humility is the exact opposite of the spirit that is proud, haughty, independent and self-sufficient.

The flesh recoils from that blessed estate of humility and brokenness. But in the light of God's promises to the broken and contrite, we do well to cultivate that kind of spirit. The process is painful, but the product is exceedingly satisfying.

We cultivate the lowly mind of brokenness when we shut ourselves away from the world, and its multiplied and strident claims, and open our hearts to God in persevering devotion. Waiting long and lovingly in His holy presence will bring us to the nadir of that circumference at the zenith of which is the Holy One that inhabiteth eternity, and we are swallowed up in the sovereign sweep of His embrace, and He dwells with us and we with Him.

The blessing of salvation comes to the broken and contrite heart (Psa. 84: 18); it is such that Jesus saves. In fact, we shall never know the joy of full salvation until first we have known the crushing sense of deep com'ic-tion that utterly subdues us.

We enter into a kinship wth Jesus when we are broken on the rack of misunderstanding, or are crushed beneath the overwhelming woe of the world in its sin. Jesus' weeping over Jerusalem is a continuing rebuke to our dry-eyed unconcern. There is a fellowship with the Saviour, all too rare in our day, and the conversation is married on in the mute but eloquent language of compassionate tears.

The blessing of conformity to the image of Christ is only to the tender and broken. Paul speaks of our being "sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise." The seal is that signet of identification, of ownership, and we know that hard wax cannot receive its impression. Only as the wax is warm and soft can it receive the image pressed upon it.

Restored fellowship is only to the broken and contrite. It was a broken man who made the zitterance recorded in our Bible as Psalm 51, David had sinner and that grievously, but there came that moment when he was plunged to the depths of contrition, and out of the depths he called upon God, pleading to be washed thoroughly from his iniquity and to be cleansed from his sin, begging that God should not take His Holy Spirit from him. This is a vastly different attitude than the one that glibly asserts that our sins, past, present and future, are all automatically under the blood. The fact is that our sins are not under the blood until our broken and contrite hearts confess them and place them there. David was speaking out of bitter and blessed experience when he said, "The sacrifices of God area broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God. thou wilt not despise."

Lessons from the realm of sports are not new. The Apostle Paul drew frequently from the games of his day to press home vital truths. He speaks of "wrestling, "running with patience the race set before us. pressing toward the mark,"

In Paul's day (and in our own) there were two groups in every contest-those who took part and those who looked on. In every figure of speech he used, the Christian was always the participant, never the spectator. The "cloud of witnesses" in Hebrews 12:1 were the Old Testament saints who had finished their course and were now looking on. But the us preferred to the believers of that clay who were to strip themselves for the race and enter it with determination.

One of the subtle dangers of present Christianity is the shift from the field of play to a seat in the grandstand. It has been that way for centuries in the Church of Rome, with relatively few taking part in the mass and many watching. The emphasis of the evangelical message on the priesthood of the believer married with it the idea that everyone was to be busy in the Lord's work. Vital religion must always require activity by all.

One attitude of the spectator" is that the payment of an admission fee entities him to look on. It may include the right to pass judgment on the plays, to jeer or cheer the players according to the measure of success that comes. That mentality can easily be married over into the Christian church. The admission fee may possibly be the whole tithe wrought into the storehouse. It may be implied from the pulpit that if all the bills are paid nothing more is demanded of the congregation. Missionary giving may be a larger development of the same false assumption that our obligation to God is discharged when we have given our money. The word program" has become a questionable badge of distinction in some circles and can unconsciously cultivate the grandstand. attitude. If UOU pay the bills we will do the work. The public service of worship degenerates into a second-rate religious raudeville. The pressure is applied for bigger and better attractions because the public is not getting its money's worth.

Another attitude of the spectator is that Very Important People can have box seats. The payment of an extra fee can secure that special privilege. The church that measures a man ' s importance by the money he gives and not by the service he renders is fitting nicely into this attitude. The wisdom and courage of the Holy Ghost were revealed in Peter when he told Simon Magnus that his money could perish with him! He hinder the operations of the Spirit. Money not only

On the way to Jerusalem. James and John, with the help of their mother. put a simple proposition to Jesus. They wanted seats in His kingdom, one on the right hand and the other on the left. Perhaps it was because they were among the first to follow Him and they felt this honor was their due. Our Lord's reply left no uncertainty as to His mind. No seats were to be assigned until the day of His reign. Then they will be given as God Himself determines.

What Christ had to offer was a cup. the symbol of His suffering. These disciples then realized how confused had been their thinking. They were willing to share that cup with Him. Paul wanted to know the fellowship of Christ's sufferings.
"They climbed the steep ascent of heaven
Through peril, toil and pain.
O God, to us may grace be given
To follow in their train."

Don't run away from your troubles. Don't magnify them. Don't dwell on them. taking them to bed with you. spoiling your digestion by feeding upon them all da>-. and willing everybody unhappy by throwing their shadow upon them. But with a resolute. courageous and trustful spirit take them to God in prayer and then go forth to meet and anguish them. and you will find they are much less formidable than you feared.

An old farmer plowed around a rock in one of his fields for many years. He had grown actually morbid over it. for he had broken a cultivator and two plows besides losing a lot of valuable land in its vicinity. One day he made up his mind that he would dig it out and have done with it. Lo, when he put his crowbar under it he found it was less thana foot thick and that he could loosen it with a trifling effort and carry it away in his wagon. He smiled to think how all through the Years it had haunted him.

One day we shall look back on our trials and our anxious cares and find how needless many of them were, so unreal and yet so distressing, that we can say like the old lady when she was reviewing her past life: "I've had so main- trials, especially those that never came. -A. B. SIX[pshN,

"Man was made to dwell in a garden,“said Dr. Hold C. Mason in a recent sermon,”but through sin he has been forced to dwell in a field, a field which he has wrested from his enemies by sweat and tears, and which he preserves only at the price of constant watchfulness and endless toil. Let him but relax his efforts for a few years and the wilderness will claim his field again. The jungle and the forest will swallow his labors and all
his loving care will have been in vain.
This is so terribly, so tragically true that we cannot resist the temptation to comment briefly upon it.

Every farmer knows the hunger of the wilderness. that hunger which no modern farm machinery, no improved agricultural methods can ever quite destroy. No matter how well prepared the soil, how well kept the fences, how carefully painted the buildings, let the owner neglect for a while his prized and valued acres and they will revert again to the wild and be swallowed up by the jungle or the wasteland. The bias of nature is toward the wilderness, never toward the fruitful field. That, we repeat, every farmer knows.

To the alert Christian this fact will be more than an observation of interest to farmers; it will be a parable, an object lesson setting forth a law that runs through all the regions of our fallen world, affecting things spiritual as well as things material. We cannot escape the law that would persuade all things to remain wild or to return to a wild state after a period of cultivation. What is true of the field is true also of the soil. if we are but wise enough to see it.

The moral bent of the fallen world is not toward godliness, but definitely away from it. "Is this vile world “help a friend of grace, asks the poet rhetorically,”to me on to God?" The sad answer is no, and it would be well for us to see that each new Christian learns this lesson as soon as possible after his conversion. We sometimes leave the impression that it is possible to find at an altar of prayer, once and for all, purity of heart and power to assure victorious living for the rest of our days. How wrong this notion is has been proved by countless numbers of Christians through the centuries.

The truth is that no spiritual experience, however revolutionary, can exempt us from temptation; and what is temptation but the effort of the wilderness to en-croach upon our new-cleared field? The purified heart is obnoxious to the devil and to all the forces of the lost world, They will not rest until they have won back what they have lost. The jungle will creep in and seek to swallow up the tiny areas that have been made free by the power of the Holy Ghost. Only watchfulness and constant prayer can preserve those moral gains won for us through the operations of God's grace.

The neglected heart will soon be a heart overrun with worldly thoughts; the neglected life will soon become a moral chaos; the church that is not jealously protected by mighty intercession and sacrificial labors will before long become the abode of every evil bird and the hiding place for unsuspected corruption, The creeping wilderness will soon take over that church that trusts In ltS own strength and forgets to watch and pray.

The law of the wilderness operates universally throughout our fallen world, on the mission Beld as well as in more sheltered lands. It is therefore an error to believe that our missionary obligation may be discharged by passing through one country after another and proclaiming the gospel without following it up with thorough teaching and careful church organization. Yet error is affecting large sections of the evangelical church, leading earnest persons to attempt to finish the evangelization of the world by this hit-and-skip method.

To make a few converts and then to leave them to their own devices without adequate care is as foolish as to turn loose a flock of newborn lambs in the middle of a wilderness; it is as absurd as to clear and plant a field in the heart of a deep woods and to leave it to the mercies of undisciplined nature. All this would be a waste of effort and could not possibly result in any real gain.

So it is with any spiritual effort that does not take into account the hunger of the wilderness. The lambs must be shepherded or they will be killed; the field must be cultivated or it will be lost; spiritual gains must be conserved by watchfulness and prayer or they too will fall victim to the enemy.
Our Lord forewarned us that false Christs should come. Mostly we think of these as coming from the outside, but we should remember that they may also arise within the sanctuary itself.

We must be extremely careful that the Christ we profess to follow is indeed the very Christ of God. There is always danger that we may be following a Christ who is not the true Christ but one conjured up by our own imagination and made in our own image.

We confess to a feeling of uneasiness about this when we observe the questionable things Christ is said to do for people these days. He is often recommended asa wonderfully obliging but not too discriminating Big Brother who delights to help us to accomplish our ends, and who further favors us by forbearing to ask any embarrassing questions about the moral and spiritual qualities of those ends.

In our eagerness to lead men to "accept Christ“we are often tempted to present for acceptance a Christ who is little more thana caricature of”that holy thing" which was conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary, to be crucified and rise the third day to take His place on the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens.

Within the past few years, for instance, Christ has been popularized by some so-called evangelicals as one who, if a proper amount of prayer were made, would help the pious prize fighter to knock another fighter unconscious in the ring. The praying gladiator then stands over his helpless foe and gazes heavenward with a radiant face while his picture is stopped for later appearance in the religious press. Christ is also said to help the big league pitcher to get the proper hook on his curve. In another instance He assists an athletically minded person to win the high jump, and still another not only to come in first in a track meet but to set a new record in the bargain. He is said also to have helped a praying businessman to beat out a competitor in a deal, to underbid a rival and to secure a coveted contract to the discomfiture of someone else who was trying to get it. He is even thought to lend succor to a praying movie actress while she plays a role so lewd as to bring the blood to the face of a professional prostitute.
Thus our Lord becomes the Christ of utility, a kind of Aladdin's lamp to do minor miracles in behalf of anyone who summons Him to do his bidding.

Apparently no one stops to consider that if Christ were to step into a prize ring and use His divine power to help one prize fighter to paralyze another He would be putting one fighter at a cruel disadvantage and,-iolating every common instinct of fair play. If He were to aid one businessman to the detriment of another He would be practicing favoritism and revealing a character wholly unlike the Bible picture of the real Christ. Furthermore, we would have the grotesque situation of the Lord of glory coming to the aid of an unreconstructed Adam-on Adam's terms.

All this is too horrible to contemplate, and we hope that the proponents of this modern accommodating Christ do not see the implications that lie in their shoddy doctrine. But perhaps they do see, and are willing nevertheless to offer this utilitarian Christ as the Saviour of mankind. If so, then they no longer believe in the deity nor the Lordship of Christ in any proper definition of those solemn words. Theirs is a Christ of carnal convenience, not too far removed from the gods of paganism.

The whole purpose of God in redemption is to make us holy and to restore us to the image of God. To accomplish this He disengages us from earthly ambitions and draws us away from the cheap and unworthy prizes that worldly men set their hearts upon. A holy man would not dream of asking God to help him beat an opponent or win over a competitor. He would not wish to succeed if to do so would mean that another man must fail. No man in whom the Spirit dwells could bring himself to ask the Lord to help him knock another man unconscious for filthy lucre or the plaudits of the vulgar spectators.

A Joshua fighting the battles of the Lord, a David rescuing God's Israel from the Philistines, a Washington seeking God's help against the enemy that would enslave the young America-this is up on a high level of moral and spiritual principle and in line with the purpose of God in human history. But to teach that Christ will use His sacred power to further our worldly interests is to wrong our Lord and injure our own souls.

We modern evangelicals need to learn the truths of the sovereignty of God and the Lordship of Christ. God will not play along with Adam; Christ will not be used by any of Adam's selfish brood. We had better learn these things fast if this generation of young Christians is to be spared the supreme tragedy of following a Christ who is merely a Christ of convenience and not the true Lord of glory after all.

The word "tribulation“comes from the Latin tribulum, meaning”a threshing sledge. The grain was spread out on the threshing floor and beaten with leather thongs fastened to a stick, called a Hail. (An older generation had some warming experiences connected with the "Rail"!) The flailing would separate the chaff from the wheat. The former would be blown away and the latter would be garnered.

The apostle seizes this figure (Rom. 5.8,4) to portray the development of the believer's post-Pentecostal life. All are in the tribulum. No one is excepted. Everyone gets Hailed. A combination of circumstances, environment, human relationships, someone to live or labor with: these are the factors that make up the tribulum experiences. Our only choice is to decide the effect tribulation will have upon us. God may not always send it; he does allow it. We may bear chastisement ks sous and accept these varied and various experiences as part of the Father's permissive providence; or, we may murmur, complain and eventrially "fail of the grace of God. By these tribulum experiences God would separate the worthless chaff from the golden wheat of our moral and spiritual soul qualities.

Patience. Tribulation has value not for what it is but for what it does. The experiences of the trib!,him, properly perceived and received, develop a character that is oxlike in patience. "Tribulation worketh [produces. begets] patience." Here is the endurance of steadfast fortitude. Patience is the virtue that continues.

And experience. Here is another child of tribulation. Approval, ripeness of character, proof of soundness: all express the thought. The idea is that of mutual fidelity to covenant engagements. God is faithful; the believer is faithful. God furnishes the grace and the believer furnishes the man. Between the two there is prepared an occupant for the mansions of light.

And hope. That which begin as tribulation now issues in hope. And it is "the hope of the glory of God. Because this hope is based. not on the whisperings of fond imaginations nor the promises of fallible fellow mortals, but on the Word of our faithful and unchanging God, it is a hope that certifies realization. Hope thou in God is at once the encouragement and incentive of Scripture. It is a hope grounded on the divine character and guaranteed by divine assurances. Men cherish expectations that never find fruition. Disappointments necessitate apologies and explanations. But our hope is not to shame us. The exultant apostle thus sings the glory' of tribulations. For here is born the God-kissed child of Patience. Experience joins the group and at last Hope completes the circle
"Tribulation worketh patience." May it be so.-H. J· s.

God's gifts are many; His best gift is one; it is the gift of Himself. Above all gifts God desires most to give Himself to His people. Our nature being what it is, we are the best fitted of all creatures to know and enjoy God. "For Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee."

When God told the Levites, "Thou shalt have no inheritance in their land...Lam thy part and thine inheritance, He in fact gave to them a portion infinitely above all the real estate in Palestine and all the earth thrown in. To possess God-this is the inheritance ultimate and supreme.

There is a sense in which God never gives any gift except He gives Himself with it. The love of God, what is it but God giving Himself in love? The mercy of God is but God giving Himself in mercy, and so with all other blessings and benefits so freely showered upon the children of atonement. Deep within all divine blessings is the Divine One Himself dwelling as in a sanctuary.

Absaloin dwelt two full years in Jerusalem and saw not the king's face, though the king was his own father. Are there not many in the kingdom of God who have no awareness of God, who seem not to know that they have the right to sit at the King's table and commune with the King? This is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is a hard and grievous burden.

To know God, this is eternal life; this is the purpose for which we are and were created. The destruction of our God-awareness was the master blow struck by Satan in the dark day of our transgression.

To give God back to us was the chief work of Christ in redemption. To impart Himself to us in personal experience is the first purpose of God in salvation. To bring acute God-awareness is the best help the Spirit brings in sanctification. All other steps in grace lead up to this.
Were we allowed but one request we might gain at a stroke all things else by praying one all-embracing prayer · " Thyself, Lord! Gice me Thyself and I can icant no more.

chapters.t: Learning to Live with Our Problems
p: As we walk the Christian way we are likely to run into three different kinds of problems: (1) problems which if we just ignore them will go away of themselves; (2) problems which we may pray our way out of, and (8) problems that will not go away and, for the time being, will not yield to the most importunate prayer.
It is the latter kind that we have in mind now.

We are all idealists. We picture to ourselves a life on earth completely free from every hindrance. a kind of spiritual Utopia where we can always control events. where we can move about as favorites of heaven, adjusting circumstances to suit ourselves. This we feel would be quite compatible with the life of faith and in keeping with the privileged place we hold as children of God.

In thinking thus we simply misplace ourselves; we mistake earth for heaven and expect conditions here below which can never be realized till we reach the better world above. While we live we may expect troubles, and plenty of them. We are never promised a life without problems as long as we remain among fallen men.

There is a sense in which God makes no difference between the saint and the sinner. I=Ie make His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. It is strange that we hardly ever notice the other side of this truth: that God also visits His children with the usual problems common to all the sous of men. The Christian will feel the heat on a sweltering day; the cold will bite into his skin as certainly as into that of his zinsaved neighbor; he will be affected by war and peace. booms and depressions, without regard to his spiritual state. To believe otherwise is to go beyond the Scriptures and to falsify the experience of the saints in ever~ age.

What then are we to do about our problems? We must learn to live with them until such time as God delivers us from them. If we cannot remove them, then we must pray for grace to endure them without murmuring. Problems patiently endured will work for our spiritual perfecting. They harm us only when we resist them or endure them unwillingly.

Our Lord was surrounded with enemies from the moment of His birth. They constituted a real lasting problem which He simply had to endure for the period of His earthly life. He escaped it only by dying.

Paul had his thorn in the flesh. We do not know for sure what it was, but it required large supplies of grace to enable him to endure it. At first he thought it belonged among the things he could pray his way out of, butt at last he was compelled to learn to live with it. The forceful masculine Paul must have been humbled br this experience. His whole temperament would lead him to attack this thing in bold determined prayer, to rush upon it like David and drive it from him for good. And that would have been a thrilling thing to do. It was less colorful to admit temporary defeat and adjust himself to the presence of an unsolved problem; but by so doing he gained a lesson he could have learned no other way. Paul was a better man for his thorn.

The pastor may expect to meet with real obstacles while he shepherds his Rock; the Christian businessman will have his troubles; the students, the housewife, the professional man, the laborer, the statesman will all feel the abrasive action of long-enduring unsolved problems.
We must both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of God. And "if thou faint in the day of adversity. thy strength is small.

In the year 1800 there was published in the city of London a little book which may easily have seta record for the length of its title. It was called A Letter to a Preacher, on IIis Entrance into the Work of the Ministry; containing Obsertations on the Most Important Subjects connected icith the Proper Discharge of the Ministerial Office: with some Directions to the People how they may Profit under the Preaching of the Word of God,

The author of this small book (only seventy printed pages) was the great Irish Wesleyan scholar and saint. Dr. Adam Charge, now famous chiefly as the author of Clarke's Commentary, an indestructible work that to this day has a place in many people's hearts. He had written a letter to a young preacher offering him a few practical suggestions. What he wrote was so good that his friends would not let it die but insisted upon his expanding it and giving it to a larger public. This he did linder the prodigious title mentioned above. Thus has this gem been preserved to us.

Beginning with this issue (page 8) we make available to our readers in three installments the sweet wisdom contained in Dr. Clarke's words. Though written a long time ago, his counsel is as fresh and modern as if he had had in mind the very day in which we live. Which may be only to say that anything great is timeless and applicable to all Christians everywhere.

chapters.t: The Cross is a Radical Thing
p: The cross of Christ is the most revolutionary thing ever to appear among mell.

The cross of old Roman times knew no compromise; it never made concessions. It won all its arguments by killing its opponent abruptly and silencing him for good. It spared not Christ, but slew Him the same as the rest. He was alive when they hung Him on that cross and completely dead when they took Him down six hours later. That was the cross the first time it appeared in Christian history.

After Christ was risen from the dead the apostles went out to preach His message, and what they preached was the cross. And wherever they went into the wide world they married the cross, and the same revolutionary power went with them. The radical message of the cross transformed Saul of Tarsus and changed him from a persecutor of Christians to a tender believer and an apostle of the faith. Its power changed bad men into good ones. It shook off the long bondage of paganism and altered completely the whole moral and mental outlook of the western world.

All this it did and continued to do as long as it was permitted to remain what it had been originally, a cross. Its power departed when it was changed from a thing of death to a thing of beauty. When men made of it a symbol, hung it around their necks as an ornament or made its outline before their faces asa magic sign to ward off evil, then it became at best a weak emblem. at worst a positive fetish. As such it is revered today by millions who know absolutely nothing about its power.

The cross effects its ends by destroying one established pattern, the victim's, and creating another pattern, its own. Thus it always has its way. It wins by defeating its opponent and imposing its will upon him. It always dominates. It never compromises, never dickers nor confers, never surrenders a point for the sake of peace. It cares not for peace; it cares only to end its opposition as fast as possible.

With perfect knowledge of all this Christ said, "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." So the cross not only brings Christ's life to an end, it ends also the first life, the old life, of every one of His true followers. It destroys the old pattern, the Adam pattern, in the believer ' s life, and brings it to an end. Then the God who raised Christ from the dead raises the believer, and a new life begins.

This, and nothing less, is true Christianity, though we cannot but recognize the sharp divergence of this conception from that held by the rank and file of evangelicals today. But we dare not qualify our position. The cross stands high above the opinions of men and to that cross all opinions must come at last for judgment. A shallow and worldly leadership would modify the cross to please the entertainment-mad saintlings who will have their fun even within the very sanctuary; but to do so is to court spiritual disaster and risk the anger of the Lamb turned Lion.

We must do something about the cross, and one of two things only we can do-Hee it or die upon it. And if we should be so foolhardy as to flee we shall by that act put away the faith of our fathers and make of Christianity something other than it is. Then we shall have left only the empty language of salvation; the power will depart with our departure from the true cross.

If we are wise we will do what Jesus did: endure the cross and despise its shame for the joy that is set before us. To do this is to submit the whole pattern of our lives to be destroyed and built again in the power of an endless life. And we shall find that it is more than poetry, more than sweet hymnody and elevated feeling. The cross will cut into our lives where it hurts worst, sparing neither us nor our carefully cultivated reputations. It will defeat us as it defeated Christ and bring our selfish lives to an end. Only then can we rise in fullness of life to establish a pattern of living wholly new and free and full of crowd 0 works.

The changed attitude toward the cross that we see in modern orthodoxy proves not that God has changed, nor that Christ has eased up on His demand that we carry the cross; it means rather that current Christianity has moved away from the standards of the New Testament. So far have we moved indeed that it may take nothing short of a new reformation to restore the cross to its right place in the theology and life of the Church.

The question is fair and the answers are many. And definitions are almost as numerous. But definitions do not tell all the story. It is like the sun; definitions here are for the Einsteins and leave the average mortal cold. So it becomes necessary to define the sun, not by what it is, but by what it does. The sun gives light and heat and produces vegetation. A child can grasp this. So with the Christian: he is best defined by attitudes and relationships.

We are agreed that one is not a Christian by virtue of negatives, be they many or beautiful. No amount of ciphers make a unit, and there are not enough negatives to make one positive. (Let us not be misunderstood: although the nondoing does not make one a Christian, there are some things that the Christian does not do. He does not practice that which he believes to be wrong. Having been saved from the past, from the penalty and power of sin, the principle of imparted righteousness causes the newborn to seek to do those things which are pleasing to his Redeemer.) The Christian is one who has had a definite, personal and satisfying transaction with Christ concerning sin and salvation. Sometime, somewhere, sin has been acknowledged, abandoned and canceled. Nothing in Christian experience is ever settled until the sin question is settled. Faith and forgiveness are joined in the holy wedlock of reconciliation and conversion becomes a reality.

The Christian having entered a new realm now lives upon a new level. His addition to the kingdom of God marks his subtraction from the kingdom of Satan. One more for the Prince of Peace spells one less for the prince of darkness. A gain for Christ is a loss for Satan. It is as Simple as that. Moral movement is not under the restraints of law; it is under the constraints of grace. The world has lost its glare and glitter, and the desire to slake one's thirst at its broken cisterns is gone-gloriously gone. Guilt is removed and the heavy weight of sin's burden is felt no more. Shackles are stopped, fetters have fallen and the soul breathes the air of freedom. The sponge of Calvary has wiped clear and clean the slate of the yesterdays and life begins with the soul's sunrise.

Having found the highway to God, the trusting heart spends time in communion with his loving Lord and those of like faith. The amount of this time is determined by the necessities of the believer's case and place, plus the circumstances and conditions of his life.

God, at long last, is recognized as the source of all blessings and gratitude is expressed in a practical manner. Since this is true, the renewed one has an earnest desire and makes some effort to extend the kingdom of God among men. This is done by life and lip, by prayer and purse, and by every other legitimate means. Having become a citizen of Immanuel's realm, the Christian exercises his franchise unto "every good word and work" and puts a premium on reaching the land of his nativity at the sunset of life.

The Christian's relationship to the household of faith is warm and generous. Sired by the same Father, redeemed by the same Saviour, born of the same Spirit and a member of the same family, the blood-washed find fellowship amd blessing in the companionship of saints. One's attitudes and adjustments toward these horizontal relationships are such that peace and harmony prevail.
Simple and elementary, you say. N<lost assuredly. But, for too long too many of us have taken too much for granted. Let's be Christian!-H. J· s.

chapters.t: The Kingdoms of the World and the Glory of Them
p: ~ ATAN once tried to bring about the downfall of Christ by offering Him all the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them.
Here is sufficient proof that the devil is wise, but not wise enough.

He knew fallen human nature and just how to handle it. He knew the power of pomp and circumstance to charm the sinful heart and bring it into captivity. In presenting to the Man Jesus the glory of the world he was shrewdly taking advantage of a known weakness in the human race. The trick should have worked, and it would have worked but for one thing: This was no fallen man Satan was attempting to seduce; it was a sinless Man full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whose penetrating glance pierced the world's attractive exterior and saw what was inside. What He saw revolted Him. He would have no part of it.

Our Lord saw in the world's glory not what other men saw and, conversely, He saw what other men could not see. He saw not beauty but death, a garish death that must be purchased at the price of the soul. Beneath its gaudy allurements He saw corruption and decay. He knew its glory was but bait to catch foolish victims. He knew its bright promises were all lies.

All this Jesus knew; and Satan for all his wisdom did not know that He knew it. The devil is an assiduous student of the Bible, but still he did not know or he would not have attempted the impossible, and that to his own confusion and permanent loss of face.

The delusive quality of all human glory is taught throughout the Bible, and with bold emphasis in the New Testament. It has been taught also with great clarity by the saints and faithful brethren since the days of the apostles. We sing it in our hymns JurE 24, 1958 and repeat it in our prayers, and no Christian but would admit the truth of it.

With the Bible open before us and a long tradition of truth behind us there would seem to be no reason for our present tragic failure to recognize the world's deceptive appeal and to stay clear of it. For there must not be any denial of the facts: the church has been captured by the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them. In spite of the prophetic voices that are raised here and there among us, present-day believers are drawn to the world with irresistible force.

That world which our Saviour once refused to buy at the price of disobedience to God is now wooing His professed followers with every sly, deceptive artifice. The glory which our Lord once rejected'with cold scorn is now being admired and sought after by multitudes who make a loud profession of accepting the gospel.
